q: 1. For cylindrical specimens, minimum strength required should be
options: 0.20 times the strength of 15 cm cubes
0.40 times the strength of 15 cm cubes
0.60 times the strength of 15 cm cubes
0.80 times the strength of 15 cm cubes
explain: The compressive strength obtained from a standard cylinder is typically about 0.80 times the strength of an equivalent 15 cm cube, due to the difference in specimen shape and testing conditions.

q: 2. The surface area of standard cube used for finding compressive strength of concrete is
explain: The standard cube face is 15cm x 15cm = 225 cm² = 22500 mm² = 0.0225 m² - all these are equivalent expressions of the same area in different units, so all of the above is correct.

q: 3. During application of load on cylindrical specimen the failure plane makes an angle of .........with the horizontal.
explain: Under compressive load, cylindrical concrete specimens typically fail along a shear plane inclined at approximately 60 degrees to the horizontal (or about 30 degrees to the vertical axis of loading).

q: 4. The ultimate load of a balanced reinforced concrete beam is proportional to
options: crushing strength of concrete and/or tensile strength of the steel
explain: In a balanced section, both the concrete's crushing (compressive) strength and the steel's tensile strength reach their limiting values simultaneously, so the ultimate load depends on both.

q: 5. The grade of concrete M 15 means that compressive strength of 15 cm cube after 28 days is
explain: By definition, the grade designation M150 directly specifies a characteristic compressive strength of 150 kg/cm² for a 15cm cube tested after 28 days.

q: 6. Allowable shear strength of concrete, depends upon
explain: The allowable shear strength of concrete is generally derived as a function of, and depends upon, its compressive strength, as per design code provisions.

q: 7. The strength of concrete is decreased by
explain: Excessive vibration (over-vibration), impact loading, and fatigue (repeated cyclic loading) can all contribute to a decrease in the effective strength of concrete over time.

q: 8. The most appropriate method to specify the concrete mix is by
explain: Specifying concrete by its grade (e.g., M20, M25) is considered the most appropriate and standardized method, as it directly denotes the required characteristic compressive strength.

q: 9. The total number of grades of ordinary concrete stipulated in IS 456:2000 are
explain: IS 456:2000 stipulates a total of 6 grades under the ordinary concrete category (M10, M15, M20, M25, M30... within the ordinary grade group).

q: 10. The standard size of a concrete cube for compressive strength test is
explain: The standard concrete cube specimen size used for compressive strength testing is 150 mm x 150 mm x 150 mm (15 cm cube).

q: 11. If the various concrete ingredients i.e. cement, sand and aggregates are in the ratio of 1:3:6, the grade of concrete, is
explain: The nominal mix ratio 1:3:6 corresponds to the M150 grade of concrete as per standard grade-mix ratio correlations.

q: 12. Permissible compressive strength of M150 concrete grade is
explain: As indicated by its designation, the M150 grade of concrete has a characteristic (permissible) compressive strength of 150 kg/cm².

q: 13. Permissible compressive strength of M150 concrete grade is
explain: 150 kg/cm² is equivalent to approximately 15 N/mm² (since 1 N/mm² ≈ 10.2 kg/cm²), making 15 N/mm² the correct equivalent expression of the M150 grade strength.

q: 14. Permissible compressive strength of M200 concrete grade is
explain: By definition, the M200 grade concrete has a characteristic (permissible) compressive strength of 200 kg/cm².

q: 15. Permissible compressive strength of M250 concrete grade is
explain: By definition, the M250 grade concrete has a characteristic (permissible) compressive strength of 250 kg/cm².

q: 16. Permissible compressive strength of M300 concrete grade is
explain: By definition, the M300 grade concrete has a characteristic (permissible) compressive strength of 300 kg/cm².

q: 17. The concrete mixes are designated into
explain: As per the classification used in this text (older IS 456 provisions), concrete mixes are designated into seven standard grades.

q: 18. Which of the following grade is not recommended by IS 456:1978
explain: M55 grade is not among the standard grades listed/recommended under the (older) IS 456:1978 provisions referenced in this text.

q: 19. Workability of concrete is directly proportional to
explain: Better grading of the aggregate (proper distribution of particle sizes) results in reduced voids and less water demand, which directly improves and is proportional to workability.

q: 20. In preliminary test, the concrete is placed in the mould in ......... layers of equal volume.
explain: As per standard cube/cylinder casting procedure for preliminary tests, concrete is placed and compacted in three equal layers.

q: 21. The preliminary test should be repeated if the difference of compressive strength of three test specimen exceeds.
explain: As per the acceptance criteria in this text, if the compressive strength results of the three test specimens vary by more than 1.5 N/mm², the preliminary test must be repeated.

q: 22. The factors which affects the design of concrete mix is
explain: Concrete mix design is influenced jointly by aggregate fineness modulus, water-cement ratio, and required workability (slump) — hence all of these factors are relevant.

q: 23. For the construction of RCC slab, column, beam and walls, the minimum grade of concrete mixed is used for
explain: The minimum recommended nominal mix for general RCC construction (slabs, columns, beams, walls) is 1:1.5:3, corresponding to M20 grade concrete. BUT AS PER OLDER CODES IT IS M 15

q: 24. M100 grade of concrete approximates
explain: The M100 grade of concrete (lowest strength grade) approximately corresponds to a lean nominal mix ratio of 1:3:6.

q: 25. The number of bags of cement required per cubic meter of 1:2:4 concrete will be approximately
explain: For a nominal 1:2:4 concrete mix, standard calculations show that approximately 4 to 5 bags of cement (50 kg each) are needed per cubic metre of concrete.

q: 26. M150 grade of concrete approximates
explain: The M150 grade of concrete approximately corresponds to a nominal mix ratio of 1:2:4 (cement:sand:aggregate).

q: 27. For batching 1:3:6 concrete mix by volume, the ingredients required per bag for 50kg cement are
options: 70 liters of sand 120 liters of aggregates
70 kg of sand 140 liters of aggregates
105 liters of sand and 140 liters of aggregates
105 liters of sand and 210 liters of aggregates
explain: For a 1:3:6 mix by volume with a standard 50 kg (35-litre volume) cement bag, the proportional quantities work out to 105 litres of sand (3 x 35) and 210 litres of aggregates (6 x 35).

q: 28. The increase in strength of concrete after 6 months
explain: As per the strength-gain data referenced in this text, concrete strength increases by about 20% beyond the 28-day value after 6 months of curing.

q: 29. The relation between modulus of rupture fcr and characteristic strength fck is given by
explain: As per IS 456, the flexural strength (modulus of rupture) of concrete is related to its characteristic compressive strength by fcr = 0.7√fck.

q: 30. The compressive strength of 100 mm cube as compared to 150 mm cube is always
explain: Due to the size effect in concrete testing, smaller 100 mm cube specimens generally record a higher apparent compressive strength than standard 150 mm cubes.

q: 31. The modulus of elasticity E of concrete can be taken as
explain: As per IS 456, the static modulus of elasticity of concrete is commonly estimated using the empirical formula E = 5700√fck (in N/mm²).

q: 32. The concrete mix which causes difficulty in obtaining a smooth finish, possess
explain: A harsh concrete mix, characterized by excessive hardness/lack of fines, makes it difficult to achieve a smooth surface finish.

q: 33. The grade of concrete not recommended by IS 456 is
explain: As per the classification referenced in this text, M30 does not appear among the listed standard grades recommended by IS 456.

q: 34. According to IS 456, the number of grades of concrete mix is
explain: As per the classification referenced in this text (older IS 456 provisions), concrete mixes are designated into seven standard grades.

q: 35. The main purpose of concrete design mix is
options: mixing the concrete in better way
explain: Design mixing proportions the ingredients scientifically to achieve the required strength and durability at the most economical cement content, making cost economy its main purpose.

q: 36. Generally nominal mix is done by volume while design mix is done by
explain: Design mixes require accurate proportioning of ingredients, which is achieved by batching materials by weight rather than the less precise volume batching used in nominal mixes.

q: 37. If the average compressive strength is 4000 kg/cm2 and standard deviation is 500, the coefficient of variation is
explain: Coefficient of variation = (standard deviation / mean) x 100 = (500/4000) x 100 = 12.5%.

q: 38. Ordinary concrete is not used for concrete grade
explain: Ordinary (nominal mix) concrete is only applicable to lower/moderate grades; higher grades like M40 require designed/controlled mix proportions and cannot use nominal mix ratios.

q: 39. Gel space ratio is defined as the ratio of
options: volume of hydrated cement to the sum of volume of hydrated cement and capillary pores
the sum of volume of hydrated cement and capillary pores to volume of hydrated cement
both a) and b) of above
explain: Gel-space ratio is defined by Powers as the volume of the gel (hydration products) divided by the sum of the volume of the gel and the capillary pore space it occupies.

q: 40. The minimum grade of concrete for pre-tensioned member is
explain: Pre-tensioned members require high early strength to allow release of the tendons, so a minimum grade of M40 concrete is specified.

q: 41. Di calcium silicate
options: provides less ultimate strength to cement
explain: Dicalcium silicate (C2S) hydrates slowly and generates comparatively less heat of hydration than tricalcium silicate, though it contributes to good long-term/ultimate strength.

q: 42. Light weight concrete is used in
explain: Because of its lower strength and density, light weight concrete finds its principal application in non-load-bearing wall construction such as partition walls.

q: 43. For reinforced concrete exposed to sulphate attack minimum grade required is
explain: As per the durability requirement referenced in this text, the minimum grade specified for reinforced concrete exposed to sulphate attack is M10.

q: 44. The total chloride content as percentage of mass of cement in concrete mix should be limited
explain: as per zonetech 0.1. As per durability provisions, the total chloride content in a concrete mix (as percentage of cement mass) should be limited to 0.16% to control the risk of reinforcement corrosion.

q: 45. The ferrocement is a composite material obtained by
options: random disposal of short, discontinuous fibres in the conventional concrete
reinforcing the cement mortar with steel fibres in the form of wire mesh
blending ferrous compounds in the ordinary Portland cement
explain: Ferrocement is defined as cement mortar reinforced with closely spaced layers of continuous, relatively thin steel wire mesh, distinguishing it from randomly dispersed fibre-reinforced concrete.

q: 46. The volume of reinforcement in ferrocement (percent) normally varies between
explain: In typical ferrocement construction, the volume fraction of the wire mesh reinforcement generally lies in the range of 5% to 8% of the total volume.

q: 47. For mass concrete in piers and abutments, the concrete mix used is of proportion.
explain: For mass concrete work such as piers and abutments, a leaner mix of proportion 1:3:6 is generally used, as high strength is not the primary requirement.

q: 48. For highly loaded columns, the concrete mix used is of proportion .........:
explain: Highly loaded columns require a rich, high-strength concrete mix, so a proportion of 1:1:2 (equivalent to a high grade) is used.

q: 49. The correct proportioning of various ingredients of concrete largely depend upon.............
explain: Correct mix proportioning must account for bulking of sand, water content, and aggregate absorption together — all of these factors affect the actual quantities batched.

q: 50. The concrete in which preliminary tests are preformed for designing the mix is called:
explain: Controlled concrete refers to concrete whose mix proportions are determined and controlled through preliminary laboratory tests to meet specified strength and durability requirements.
